tool.name: Bash
tool.tagline: The standard Unix shell for running commands and writing scripts
tool.description: Bash (the Bourne Again SHell) is the command interpreter on most Linux systems and the language of countless build, deploy and automation scripts. It glues programs together with pipes, redirection and variables, and adds loops, functions and arrays for real scripting. Knowing it well makes you faster at the terminal and lets you read and write the scripts that run CI pipelines, containers and servers.

glossary.def: A command built into Bash itself, such as cd or echo, rather than a separate program file on disk.
In Bash, a short name you define for a longer command, e.g. alias ll='ls -l' lets you type ll instead.
The first line of a script, starting with #!, that names the program which should run the rest of the file, e.g. #!/usr/bin/env bash.
Bash replacing something you typed with its value before running the command: $name becomes the variable's value, *.txt becomes the matching file names.
Bash cutting the result of an unquoted $ expansion into separate words at spaces, tabs and line breaks. Double quotes prevent it.
In Bash, a text pattern with wildcards, like *.txt or report-??.csv: * matches any characters, ? exactly one. Used to match file names and text.
Bash turning {a,b,c} into a b c and {1..5} into 1 2 3 4 5, a quick way to write lists and ranges.
The arguments a script or function receives, available as $1, $2 and so on; $# says how many there are and "$@" gives them all.
A variable Bash fills in for you, such as $? (the last command's exit status), $# (number of arguments) or $$ (the shell's process ID).
The ${...} forms that read a variable and change the value on the way, e.g. ${name:-default} or ${file%.txt}.
Writing $(command) to run a command and use its output as text in another command, e.g. today=$(date).
Writing $(( ... )) to have Bash calculate whole-number maths, e.g. $(( 2 + 3 )) becomes 5.
A separate copy of the running shell that Bash starts for ( ), $( ), pipeline parts and background jobs. Changes made inside it are lost when it ends.
Lines of text written directly in a script after <<WORD, up to a line containing just WORD, and fed to a command as its input.
Writing <<< "text" to feed one piece of text to a command as its input.
Bash's internal field separator: a variable listing the characters (normally space, tab and newline) used to split text into words and fields.
The first shell started when you log in (for example over SSH). It reads different startup files from the shells you open afterwards.
A file of commands Bash runs when it starts, such as ~/.bashrc or ~/.bash_profile, used for your settings, aliases and PATH.
The common Bash settings set -euo pipefail, which make a script stop at the first failed command, unset variable or failed pipeline part.
A Bash command that registers code to run when the script exits or receives a signal, typically used to clean up.
A short notice the operating system delivers to a running program, such as 'stop now' (Ctrl-C) or 'please finish up'. Programs can react to most signals.
A Bash-only event a trap can react to as if it were a signal, such as EXIT (the script is ending) or ERR (a command failed).
Writing <(command) so a command's output can be used where a file name is expected, e.g. diff <(sort a) <(sort b).
The shell features for managing commands running in the background: jobs, fg, bg and Ctrl-Z.
How a program starts a new process on Linux and macOS: it makes a copy of itself, which can then turn into another program (exec).
Replacing a running process's program with another one, keeping the same process ID; also the Bash command that does this to the shell.
A feature that works in Bash but not in the plain POSIX sh shell, such as [[ ]] or arrays.
A Bash array that maps names (keys) to values, like port[http]=80, instead of numbering its items.
A free tool that reads shell scripts without running them and warns about common mistakes, such as missing quotes.

concepts.name: The shell and running commands
concepts.summary: What a terminal and a shell are, how a typed line splits into a command and its arguments, and how to get help.
concepts.why: Every other shell skill builds on reading and typing commands correctly.
concepts.body:
Most of the time you use a computer by clicking. A **terminal** is the other way in: a window where you type an instruction, press Enter, and the computer answers in text. The program inside the terminal that reads your line and carries it out is called the **shell**. Bash is the most common shell: it's the standard one on Linux, and macOS's own shell (zsh) behaves almost the same for everything in these lessons.

When the shell is ready, it shows a short prompt, often ending in `$`. You type a line after it and press Enter, and the shell runs it.

Bash splits the line you typed into words wherever there are spaces. The first word is the **command**: the name of the program to run. The other words are its **arguments** (also called command-line arguments): extra information for the command, such as which file to work on. In `ls -l Documents`, the command is `ls` (list files) and its arguments are `-l` and `Documents`.

Arguments that start with a dash are **options**, switches that change how the command behaves. Short options are a single letter (`-l`), long ones are whole words (`--all`), and short ones can often be bundled: `ls -la` means `ls -l -a`.

Two more characters to know: `;` separates several commands on one line, and `#` starts a **comment**, a note for people that the shell ignores.

Commands come in a few kinds, and `type name` tells you which:

- a **builtin**, such as `cd` (change folder) or `echo` (print text), built into bash itself;
- an **alias** or function: a shortcut name you or your settings created;
- a separate program file. Bash finds it by looking through a list of folders called the **PATH**.

For help, run `help name` for builtins, and `man name` (the manual) or `name --help` for programs. A few keys save lots of typing: Tab completes commands and file names, Up and Down step through earlier commands, Ctrl-R searches them, Ctrl-C stops the command that's running, and Ctrl-L clears the screen.
concepts.code:
echo hello   world          # hello world   (extra spaces just separate words)
type cd                     # cd is a shell builtin
type ls                     # ls is /usr/bin/ls   (a program file)
help echo                   # short help for the echo builtin
ls -la /tmp                 # long listing of all files: -l and -a bundled
date; pwd                   # two commands: today's date, then the current folder
# everything after # is a comment
takeaways: A typed command = the command's name + its arguments, split at spaces
type tells you whether a name is a builtin, alias, function or program
help for builtins; man or --help for programs
pitfalls: Expecting several spaces between arguments to be kept: spaces outside quotes only separate words.

quiz.q: Which command tells you whether cd is a builtin or a program on disk?
quiz.explain: type knows about builtins, aliases and functions; which only searches the PATH folders.

quiz.q: How many arguments does `ls -l  /tmp   /var` pass to ls?
quiz.explain: The words after the command are -l, /tmp and /var; extra spaces only separate words.

concepts.name: Variables
concepts.summary: Store text in named variables, read it back with $, and meet the special variables bash fills in for you.
concepts.why: Variables hold file names, folders and settings, so you write them once and reuse them everywhere.
takeaways: name=value with no spaces; read it with "$name" or "${name}"
Bash variables hold text; do arithmetic inside $(( ))
Unset variables silently become empty text
Lower-case for your own variables, UPPER_CASE for environment ones
pitfalls: Writing `x = 5`: bash runs a command named x with arguments = and 5.

quiz.q: What does `greeting = hi` do in bash?
options: Runs a command named greeting with two arguments
quiz.explain: Spaces make it a normal command line: the command is greeting, the arguments are = and hi.

quiz.q: After `v=10`, what does `echo "$v1"` print?
quiz.explain: Bash looks for a variable named v1, which is unset and expands to nothing; write ${v}1 for 101.

concepts.name: Quoting: single, double and none
concepts.summary: How single quotes, double quotes and backslashes control which characters bash treats specially.
concepts.why: Missing quotes around variables are the most common source of shell mistakes, from broken file names to deleted data.
concepts.body:
Spaces separate the words of a command, and that causes trouble with values that contain spaces. Say `file="my report.txt"`. Then `rm $file` (`rm` deletes files) gives `rm` two arguments, `my` and `report.txt`, so it tries to delete two files that don't exist, or worse, two that do.

Here's why. After bash expands a variable that isn't inside quotes, it does two more things to the result. First, **word splitting**: it cuts the value into separate words at spaces, tabs and line breaks.

Second, **globbing**: it treats `*`, `?` and `[...]` as a **pattern** for file names. `*` stands for any characters, so `*.txt` turns into the names of every file ending in `.txt`.

Quotes switch both off:

- **Double quotes** `"..."` keep the text as one word but still expand variables like `$var` (and the other `$` forms you'll meet later). Use them around nearly every `$`: `"$file"`.
- **Single quotes** `'...'` change nothing inside: `'$HOME'` stays exactly `$HOME`. A single quote can't appear inside them.
- A **backslash** protects the next character: `echo \$HOME` prints `$HOME`.
- `$'...'` understands codes like `\n` (new line) and `\t` (tab).

Quotes can be mixed in one word: `'It'\''s'` or `"$name"'s file'`. They are removed before the command sees its arguments, so `echo "a"b'c'` receives the single argument `abc`.

The rule of thumb is simple: **put double quotes around every `$`**, unless you deliberately want splitting or globbing.
concepts.code:
cd "$(mktemp -d)"           # go into a fresh, empty practice folder
file="my report.txt"
touch "$file"               # create an empty file with that name
ls $file          # ls: cannot access 'my' ... and 'report.txt' (two words!)
ls "$file"        # my report.txt
echo '$HOME is literal'     # $HOME is literal
echo "Home is $HOME"        # Home is /home/you
echo \$HOME                 # $HOME
echo $'col1\tcol2'          # col1    col2
star="*"
echo $star        # my report.txt   (the * matched the file names!)
echo "$star"      # *
echo "a"b'c'      # abc  (quotes are removed, pieces join)
takeaways: Unquoted variables are split at spaces, and * or ? in them match file names
Double quotes: one word, variables still expand; single quotes: nothing changes
Default to "$var" everywhere
pitfalls: Writing rm $file without quotes when the file name can contain spaces, or be empty.

quiz.q: With `f="a b"`, how many arguments does `touch $f` pass to touch?
quiz.explain: Without quotes, the value is split at the space into a and b.

quiz.q: What does `echo '$USER'` print?
quiz.explain: Single quotes stop all expansion, and the quotes themselves are removed.

concepts.name: Exit status, && and ||
concepts.summary: Every command reports a number when it finishes: 0 means success. Run the next command only on success or failure with && and ||.
concepts.why: Exit statuses are how the shell notices errors and decides what to run next.
concepts.body:
When a command finishes, it reports a number to the shell: its **exit status** (also called exit code). **0 means success**; anything from 1 to 255 means some kind of failure. Each program documents its own failure numbers. For example `grep`, which searches text, returns 1 for "not found" and 2 for a real error.

The status of the last command is kept in `$?`. Read it straight away, because the next command replaces it.

Bash lets you run a command depending on that status:

- `a && b` runs `b` only if `a` succeeded,
- `a || b` runs `b` only if `a` failed,
- `! a` flips the status: success becomes failure and the other way round.

So `mkdir -p out && cd out` (make a folder, then go into it) only goes into the folder if creating it worked. And `command -v jq || echo "please install jq"` checks that the program `jq` is installed, and complains if it isn't. You can combine them, but `a && b || c` is not a true "if this, otherwise that": `c` also runs when `b` fails.

Your own scripts (files of commands, covered soon) end with the status of the last command they ran, or the number you give `exit`. Use `exit 0` for success and a small non-zero number, often 1, for failure, so whatever started the script can tell what happened. `true` and `false` are commands that do nothing but succeed (0) and fail (1).
concepts.code:
grep -q root /etc/passwd      # quietly search the system's user list
echo $?                       # 0  (found)
grep -q nosuchuser /etc/passwd
echo $?                       # 1  (not found)
ls /nope 2>/dev/null; echo $? # 2  (an error; 2>/dev/null hides its message)
mkdir -p build && echo "created"     # created
false || echo "fallback ran"         # fallback ran
! true; echo $?               # 1  (! flips the status)
true; false; echo $?          # 1  (only the last command counts)
command -v git >/dev/null && echo "git is installed"   # >/dev/null hides output
takeaways: 0 = success, 1-255 = failure; $? holds the last status
&& runs on success, || on failure, ! flips the status
End scripts with a meaningful exit code
pitfalls: Using `a && b || c` as if it meant 'if a then b, otherwise c': c also runs when b fails.

quiz.q: What is printed by `false; true; echo $?`?
quiz.explain: $? is the status of the most recent command, true, which returns 0.

quiz.q: In `mkdir out && cd out || echo failed`, when is 'failed' printed?
options: If either mkdir or cd fails
quiz.explain: || reacts to the status of the whole && part before it, so a failure of either command triggers it.

concepts.name: Writing and running a script
concepts.summary: Put commands in a file with a shebang line, make it runnable and read the arguments it's given.
concepts.why: Scripts turn a sequence of commands you keep retyping into a reusable tool.
concepts.body:
A **script** is a text file full of commands that bash runs one after another. A sequence you keep retyping becomes one reusable tool. Write it in any **text editor** (a program for editing text without formatting, such as Notepad or nano) and save it with a name ending in `.sh`.

Its first line should be a **shebang**: `#!/usr/bin/env bash`. It tells the computer which program should read the rest of the file, here bash, wherever it is installed.

Before you can run a file directly, mark it as runnable, or **executable**, once: `chmod +x greet.sh`. Then run it as `./greet.sh`. The `./` means "the file in this folder": for a bare name, bash only searches the PATH folders, and the folder you're in isn't one of them. Alternatively, `bash greet.sh` runs the file without marking it.

Words typed after the script's name arrive inside it as **positional parameters**:

- `$1`, `$2`, ... the arguments; from the tenth on, write `${10}`;
- `$#` how many arguments there are, `$0` the name the script was started with;
- `"$@"` all the arguments, each kept as a separate word: the right way to pass them on to another command.

`${2:-Hello}` means "the second argument, or Hello if it's missing or empty"; you'll meet more of these forms later.

A script runs as its own **process**: a separate running copy of bash, started for the script and gone when it finishes. So a `cd` or a variable set inside the script doesn't affect your terminal afterwards. Use `source greet.sh` when you do want the commands to run in your current shell.

Name scripts clearly, put a usage comment at the top, and `exit` with a non-zero status on errors.
concepts.code:
cd "$(mktemp -d)"           # go into a fresh, empty practice folder
# write the lines up to EOF into greet.sh (or use a text editor)
cat > greet.sh <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# usage: greet.sh NAME [GREETING]
name=$1
greeting=${2:-Hello}
echo "$greeting, $name! ($# args, called as $0)"
EOF
chmod +x greet.sh
./greet.sh Ada              # Hello, Ada! (1 args, called as ./greet.sh)
./greet.sh Bob "Hi there"   # Hi there, Bob! (2 args, called as ./greet.sh)
bash greet.sh Cy            # Hello, Cy! (1 args, called as greet.sh)
takeaways: Start with #!/usr/bin/env bash and chmod +x the file
$1..$9, ${10}, $# and "$@" give you the arguments
A script runs as its own process; source it to affect your current shell
pitfalls: Running `script.sh` without ./ and getting 'command not found', because the current folder isn't on the PATH.

quiz.q: Inside a script called as `./s.sh a "b c"`, what is $#?
quiz.explain: "b c" is quoted, so it is a single argument; there are two.

quiz.q: A script does `cd /tmp`. Why is your terminal still in the old directory afterwards?
options: The script ran as a separate process
quiz.explain: Each script gets its own process with its own current folder; use source to run it in your current shell.

concepts.name: if and test conditions
concepts.summary: Make decisions with if/elif/else, using [[ ]] tests on text, numbers and files, and (( )) for arithmetic.
concepts.why: Checking that files exist, values are present or text matches is how commands make decisions.
concepts.body:
`if` runs a command and, if its exit status is 0 (success), runs the commands after `then`. Otherwise it tries the next `elif` ("else if"), and finally `else`. The full shape is `if cond; then ...; elif cond; then ...; else ...; fi`, where `fi` ("if" backwards) closes it.

The condition is usually a test written in brackets:

- `[[ ... ]]` is bash's own test. Variables inside aren't split into words, you can combine checks with `&&` and `||`, `==` compares text against a pattern like `*.csv`, and `=~` against a **regular expression**, a more powerful text-matching language. Prefer it in bash.
- `[ ... ]` is the older test that every shell has. It is actually a command named `[`, so it needs spaces inside the brackets and quotes around variables.
- `(( ... ))` does arithmetic and succeeds when the result isn't zero, so `(( n > 5 ))` works as you'd expect.

Common tests: text `-z` (empty), `-n` (not empty), `==`, `!=`; numbers `-eq -ne -lt -le -gt -ge` (equal, not equal, less than, less or equal, greater than, greater or equal), or `<` and `>` inside `(( ))`; files `-e` exists, `-f` is a normal file, `-d` is a folder, `-r -w -x` you may read / change / run it, `-s` isn't empty.

Any command works as a condition: `if grep -q error log.txt; then` (`-q` means quietly: print nothing, just report found or not) runs the `then` part when the file contains "error". That's simpler and faster than saving the output and checking it.

Watch out: inside `[[ ]]`, `<` and `>` compare **text** in alphabetical order, so `[[ 10 < 9 ]]` is true ("1" comes before "9"). Use `-lt` or `(( ))` for numbers. After an `=~` match, the matched pieces are in `BASH_REMATCH`.
concepts.code:
f=/etc/passwd
if [[ -d $f ]]; then
  echo "$f is a directory"
elif [[ -f $f && -r $f ]]; then
  echo "$f is a readable file"     # this branch runs
else
  echo "$f: not found"
fi
name=""
[[ -z $name ]] && echo "name is empty"            # name is empty
n=7
if (( n > 5 )); then echo "big"; fi              # big
if [ "$n" -lt 10 ]; then echo "single digit"; fi # single digit
s="report.csv"
[[ $s == *.csv ]] && echo "CSV file"             # CSV file
[[ $s =~ ^([a-z]+)\. ]] && echo "${BASH_REMATCH[1]}"   # report  (letters before the dot)
[[ 10 < 9 ]] && echo "string comparison!"        # string comparison!
takeaways: if runs the then part when the condition command exits 0
Prefer [[ ]] for strings and files, (( )) for numbers
Any command can be a condition: if grep -q ...; then
pitfalls: Comparing numbers with < or == inside [[ ]], which compares them as strings.

quiz.q: What does `[[ 10 < 9 ]]` return?
quiz.explain: Inside [[ ]], < compares text in dictionary order; use -lt or (( )) for numbers.

quiz.q: Which test is true when $dir names an existing directory?
quiz.explain: -d checks for a folder; -n only checks that the text isn't empty.

concepts.name: for and while loops
concepts.summary: Repeat commands for every item in a list, file pattern or number range, or while a condition holds, with for, while and until.
concepts.why: Loops let one command handle every file, folder or line instead of one at a time.
concepts.body:
A **loop** repeats commands. The **for** loop runs once for each word in a list: `for x in a b c; do ...; done` runs the commands between `do` and `done` three times, with `$x` set to `a`, then `b`, then `c`.

The list is usually a pattern like `*.txt` (every matching file name), or a range like `{1..10}` or a list like `{a,b,c}`, which bash writes out for you; that's called **brace expansion**. Don't loop over the output of `ls`: file names with spaces get split into pieces. Use a pattern instead.

If a pattern matches nothing, bash leaves the pattern itself as the only word (`*.txt`). Protect against that with `[[ -e $f ]] || continue`, or switch on `shopt -s nullglob` so it produces no words at all.

The counting loop `for ((i = 0; i < n; i++))` is handy for counters (`i++` adds one to `i`). **while** repeats as long as its condition command succeeds, and **until** repeats until it succeeds. That suits waiting for something: `until [[ -f ready.txt ]]; do sleep 1; done` checks once a second until the file exists.

Inside any loop, `break` leaves it and `continue` skips to the next round. You can also send a whole loop's output somewhere at once: `done > out.txt` writes everything the loop prints into one file (`>` is explained in the Redirection lesson).
concepts.code:
cd "$(mktemp -d)" && touch a.txt b.txt   # practice folder with two files
for fruit in apple "star fruit" kiwi; do
  echo "- $fruit"
done                         # - apple / - star fruit / - kiwi
for f in *.txt; do
  [[ -e $f ]] || continue    # skip the leftover '*.txt' if nothing matched
  echo "found $f"
done                         # found a.txt / found b.txt
for ((i = 1; i <= 3; i++)); do echo "i=$i"; done      # i=1 / i=2 / i=3
for n in {1..5}; do echo -n "$n "; done; echo        # 1 2 3 4 5
count=0
while (( count < 3 )); do
  count=$(( count + 1 ))
done
echo "count=$count"          # count=3
until [[ -f ready ]]; do touch ready; done && echo "ready"      # ready
takeaways: for x in words / *.txt / {1..5}; for ((...)) for counters
while repeats while the condition succeeds, until until it does
Loop over patterns like *.txt, never over the output of ls
pitfalls: Forgetting that a pattern that matches nothing stays as it is, so the loop runs once with '*.txt'.

quiz.q: In an empty directory, how many times does `for f in *.log; do echo "$f"; done` print, by default?
quiz.explain: Without nullglob, a pattern that matches nothing stays as it is, so the loop runs once with the pattern itself.

quiz.q: Which loop keeps retrying a command until it succeeds?
quiz.explain: until runs the body while the condition fails and stops on the first success.

concepts.name: Redirection: >, >>, 2> and <
concepts.summary: Save a command's output and error messages in files, feed files in as input, and throw away unwanted output.
concepts.why: Saving output, keeping error messages and feeding files into commands are everyday shell tasks.
concepts.body:
Every running program has three standard streams of text. **Standard input** is where it reads from, normally your keyboard. **Standard output** is where its normal results go, normally your screen. **Standard error** is a separate stream for error messages, which also shows on your screen.

Each stream has a number: 0 for input, 1 for output, 2 for errors. You'll see those numbers in the redirection signs below. **Redirection** means connecting a stream to a file instead, before the command starts:

- `> file` writes standard output to a file, **emptying the file first**; `>> file` adds to the end instead.
- `2> file` writes error messages to a file; `2>> file` adds to the end.
- `2>&1` points errors to wherever output is going right now; `&> file` is bash's shorthand for "both into the file".
- `< file` feeds the file in as standard input.
- `/dev/null` is a special file that throws away whatever is written to it.

Redirections happen **left to right**, so order matters. `cmd > out.txt 2>&1` puts both into the file. But `cmd 2>&1 > out.txt` first points errors at the screen (where output was going at that moment) and only then points output at the file.

Put your own error messages on standard error too: `echo "error: missing file" >&2`. Then someone can save your normal output to a file and still see the errors on screen.

Beware `sort data.txt > data.txt`: the shell empties the file before `sort` reads it, so you end up with nothing. Write to a new file and rename it afterwards. `set -o noclobber` makes `>` refuse to overwrite existing files.
concepts.code:
cd "$(mktemp -d)"             # fresh, empty practice folder
echo "first" > out.txt        # create (or empty) the file, then write
echo "second" >> out.txt      # add to the end
cat out.txt                   # first / second
ls /nope 2> err.txt           # the error message goes to the file
cat err.txt                   # ls: cannot access '/nope': No such file or directory
ls /tmp /nope > all.txt 2>&1  # output and errors into the file
ls /tmp /nope &> all.txt      # bash shorthand for the same
wc -l < out.txt               # 2  (count lines; no file name printed)
ls /nope 2>/dev/null || echo "quietly failed"   # quietly failed
echo "error: something broke" >&2               # write to standard error
takeaways: 0 = input, 1 = output, 2 = errors; > replaces a file, >> adds to it
cmd > file 2>&1 puts both in the file; the order of redirections matters
Write your own error messages to >&2
pitfalls: `sort f > f` empties the file: the shell empties it before sort reads it.

quiz.q: Which line writes both the normal output and the error messages of cmd into log.txt?
quiz.explain: Redirections run left to right: first output goes to the file, then errors are pointed at the same place.

quiz.q: What does `wc -l < notes.txt` print compared with `wc -l notes.txt`?
options: Only the count, without the file name
quiz.explain: With <, wc just receives the text and never learns the file's name.

concepts.name: Pipelines
concepts.summary: Connect commands with | so each one's output becomes the next one's input.
concepts.why: Pipelines let small tools team up into powerful one-line commands for searching, counting and reshaping text.
concepts.code:
printf '%s\n' banana apple cherry apple | sort | uniq -c   # one word per line, sorted, counted
#   2 apple
#   1 banana
#   1 cherry
seq 1 100 | tail -n 3 | awk '{ s += $1 } END { print s }'   # 297  (awk adds up 98+99+100)
cut -d: -f7 /etc/passwd | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -n 3   # most common login shells
ls /nope 2>&1 | wc -l          # 1  (the error message went into the pipe)
ls /nope |& wc -l              # 1  (bash shorthand)
false | true; echo $?          # 0  (status of the LAST command)
false | true; echo "${PIPESTATUS[@]}"   # 1 0
yes | head -n 2                # y / y  (yes stops once head has quit)
takeaways: a | b feeds a's output into b's input; all parts run at the same time
Use 2>&1 | or |& to send error messages through too
A pipeline's status is the last command's unless pipefail is set
pitfalls: Assuming `cmd | tee log` fails when cmd fails: without pipefail it reports tee's success.

quiz.q: What is the exit status of `false | true` without pipefail?
options: It depends on the shell options of false
quiz.explain: Without pipefail, a pipeline returns the status of its last command, true.

quiz.q: Why does `yes | head -n 2` finish even though yes never ends on its own?
options: head stops it with a forced kill
yes gets SIGPIPE when writing to a closed pipe
quiz.explain: After head exits, nobody reads the pipe any more, so yes's next write gets the SIGPIPE signal and it stops.

concepts.name: Parameter expansion tricks
concepts.summary: Give variables defaults, cut pieces off their values, search and replace, and change letter case, all inside ${...}.
concepts.why: These forms replace many calls to separate tools like sed, basename and dirname, so scripts get shorter and faster.
concepts.body:
`${...}` can do much more than read a variable: it can change the value on the way out. This is called **parameter expansion**. The forms you will use constantly:

- **Defaults**: `${var:-def}` gives `def` if var is unset or empty; `${var:=def}` also assigns it; `${var:?message}` aborts the script with the message; `${var:+alt}` gives `alt` only when var is set.
- **Cut a pattern off the start or end**: `#` removes the shortest matching start, `##` the longest; `%` and `%%` do the same at the end. So `${path##*/}` is the file name without its folders, `${path%/*}` is the folder part, and `${file%.*}` drops the ending such as `.txt`.
- **Replace**: `${var/old/new}` first match, `${var//old/new}` all matches; these are bash patterns, not regular expressions.
- **Length and pieces**: `${#var}` is the number of characters; `${var:start:length}` takes a piece, counting positions from 0; count from the end with a space before the minus: `${var: -3}`.
- **Case** (bash 4+): `${var^}` capitalizes the first letter, `${var^^}` upper-cases all, `${var,,}` lower-cases.

Without the colon (`${var-def}`) the default applies only when var is **unset**, not when it is empty. That distinction matters for optional settings where an empty value is meaningful.

These expansions run inside the shell, so they are much faster than starting a separate program like `basename` or `sed` for every item.
concepts.code:
path="/var/log/nginx/access.log.gz"
echo "${path##*/}"        # access.log.gz        (basename)
echo "${path%/*}"         # /var/log/nginx       (dirname)
echo "${path%.gz}"        # /var/log/nginx/access.log
echo "${path#*.}"         # log.gz               (up to the first dot)
echo "${#path}"           # 28
echo "${path/log/LOG}"    # /var/LOG/nginx/access.log.gz
echo "${path//log/LOG}"   # /var/LOG/nginx/access.LOG.gz
echo "${path:5:3}"        # log
echo "${path: -2}"        # gz
unset port
echo "${port:-8080}"      # 8080  (port is still unset)
echo "${port:=3000} $port"     # 3000 3000
name=ada
echo "${name^} ${name^^}" # Ada ADA
# : "${API_KEY:?must be set}"  -> aborts: API_KEY: must be set
takeaways: ${v:-def} default, ${v:=def} assign, ${v:?msg} require
# and ## strip prefixes, % and %% strip suffixes
${v//a/b} replaces using patterns; ${#v} is the length
pitfalls: Writing ${var:-3} when you meant the last 3 characters: you need ${var: -3} with a space.

quiz.q: With f=archive.tar.gz, what is ${f%%.*}?
quiz.explain: %% removes the longest suffix matching .*, which starts at the first dot.

quiz.q: What does ${name:-guest} give when name is set to the empty string?
quiz.explain: The colon form treats empty the same as unset; ${name-guest} would give the empty string.

concepts.name: Command substitution and arithmetic
concepts.summary: Capture a command's output with $(...) and do whole-number maths with $(( )) and (( )).
concepts.why: Commands constantly need dates, counts and computed values from other commands.
concepts.body:
**Command substitution** `$(command)` runs the command and puts what it printed (its standard output) in its place, minus any line breaks at the very end. Use it to store results: `today=$(date +%F)`, `n=$(wc -l < file)`. An older form with backticks does the same but is hard to nest; prefer `$( )`, which nests cleanly: `$(dirname "$(readlink -f "$0")")`.

Quote the substitution when using it as an argument, `"$(cmd)"`, or the output will be word-split and pattern-matched like any unquoted expansion. In a plain assignment `x=$(cmd)` no quotes are needed, but they do no harm.

**Arithmetic expansion** `$(( expr ))` does whole-number maths with `+ - * / % **` (`%` is the remainder after dividing, `**` is "to the power of"), comparisons, `&&`, `||` and a few more. Variables inside need no `$`. Division drops the fraction, and bash has **no decimal numbers** at all, so use `awk` or `bc` when you need them.

The command form `(( expr ))` calculates without printing anything and succeeds when the result isn't zero, which makes it ideal for conditions and counters: `(( count++ ))`, `if (( n % 2 == 0 ))`. Note that `(( x++ ))` counts as a failure when x was 0, which matters in strict mode (a later lesson); write `x=$(( x + 1 ))` there.

Numbers with a leading zero, like `08`, are read as base 8 (octal) and fail; strip the zeros, or write `10#$n` to force base 10.
concepts.code:
today=$(date +%F)
entries=$(ls / | wc -l)
echo "Today is $today; / has $entries entries"
kernel="$(uname -r)"
echo "Running kernel $kernel"
lines=$(printf 'a\nb\n\n\n')   # trailing newlines are stripped
echo "${#lines}"               # 3  ("a", newline, "b")
x=7 y=3
echo $(( x * y + 1 ))          # 22
echo $(( x / y )) $(( x % y )) # 2 1   (integers only)
echo $(( 2 ** 10 ))            # 1024
(( x > y )) && echo "x wins"   # x wins
month=08
echo $(( 10#$month + 1 ))      # 9   (force base 10, avoid octal)
awk 'BEGIN { printf "%.2f\n", 10 / 3 }'   # 3.33  (floats need another tool)
takeaways: $(cmd) captures a command's output without trailing line breaks; quote it as an argument
$(( )) for whole-number maths, (( )) for arithmetic conditions
No decimals in bash: use awk or bc
pitfalls: Leading zeros: $(( 08 + 1 )) fails because 08 is read as an invalid base-8 number.

quiz.q: What does `echo $(( 7 / 2 ))` print?
quiz.explain: Bash arithmetic uses whole numbers only, and division drops the fraction.

quiz.q: Why prefer $(...) over backticks?
quiz.explain: Both capture output, but $(...) can be nested without escaping and is easier to read.

concepts.name: Functions
concepts.summary: Bundle commands into named, reusable functions with their own arguments, local variables, status and output.
concepts.why: Functions keep scripts readable and testable instead of one long list of commands.
concepts.body:
A **function** is a named group of commands you can run like any other command. Define it with `name() { commands; }` and call it: `name arg1 arg2`. Inside, the arguments are `$1`, `$2`, `$#` and `"$@"`, just like in a script; `$0` still names the script.

Variables are **global by default**: a function that sets `i` changes the caller's `i` too. Declare working variables with `local` so they exist only while the function runs (functions it calls can still see them).

Functions "return" things in two ways:

- **Status**: `return N` (0-255), or else the status of the last command. This is for success or failure, so a function like `is_even` can be used directly in `if`.
- **Data**: print it to standard output and capture it with `result=$(myfunc)`. Write messages and errors to standard error (`>&2`) so they don't end up in the captured result.

Capturing with `$( )` runs the function in a **subshell**, a separate copy of the shell, so variable changes inside it are lost. If you need to set a caller's variable, use a global one, or a name reference (`local -n ref=$1`, bash 4.3+).

Define functions before calling them, because bash reads scripts from top to bottom. A common layout is: settings, then functions, then a single `main "$@"` call at the very end. That also stops a half-downloaded script from running only partly.
concepts.code:
log() { printf '[%s] %s\n' "$(date +%T)" "$*" >&2; }
max() {
  local a=$1 b=$2            # local: invisible outside the function
  if (( a > b )); then echo "$a"; else echo "$b"; fi
}
is_even() { (( $1 % 2 == 0 )); }    # status of last command = result
set_var() { local -n ref=$1; ref=$2; }   # nameref: write caller's variable
main() {
  log "starting"             # [12:00:00] starting  (on stderr)
  local biggest
  biggest=$(max 4 9)         # data comes back via stdout
  echo "max=$biggest"        # max=9
  if is_even 10; then echo "10 is even"; fi   # 10 is even
  is_even 7 || echo "7 is odd"                # 7 is odd
  set_var color blue; echo "color=$color"     # color=blue
}
main "$@"
takeaways: name() { ...; } with $1, $2, "$@" for arguments
Use local for every working variable
return is a status; output data on stdout and capture with $( )
pitfalls: Using `return "$value"` to return data: it is a 0-255 status number, not a value.

quiz.q: A function sets `count=5` without local. What happens to a global count?
quiz.explain: Variables in bash functions are global unless declared local.

quiz.q: How should a function hand a string result to its caller?
quiz.explain: return only carries a 0-255 status; printing and capturing is the usual way to hand back data.

concepts.name: Indexed and associative arrays
concepts.summary: Keep lists of values, and tables of names to values, in arrays; loop over them safely and pass them on intact.
concepts.why: Arrays are the only safe way to hold lists of file names or arguments that may contain spaces.
concepts.body:
An **array** is a variable that holds a list of values. Create one with `arr=(a "b c" d)` and add to it with `arr+=(e)`. Items are numbered from 0, and that number is called the **index**: `${arr[1]}` is `b c`. The essential forms:

- `"${arr[@]}"` every item as a separate word (always quote it),
- `${#arr[@]}` the number of items, `${!arr[@]}` the indexes in use,
- `"${arr[@]:1:2}"` a slice: two items starting at index 1.

Arrays can have gaps (they are *sparse*): after `unset 'arr[0]'` the indexes are 1 2 3. So loop over the items, or over `${!arr[@]}`, rather than assuming 0 to n-1.

**Associative arrays** (bash 4+) use names, called keys, instead of numbers, and must be declared: `declare -A port=([http]=80 [https]=443)`. Set with `port[ssh]=22`, read with `${port[ssh]}`, list the keys with `"${!port[@]}"`. Keys come back in no particular order, so sort them if you need stable output. Test for a key with `[[ -v port[ssh] ]]`.

Arrays shine for building command lines: `args=(--verbose); [[ $dry ]] && args+=(--dry-run); rsync "${args[@]}" src/ dst/` passes each option as exactly one argument, which gluing text together can't do safely.

To read the lines of a file or command into an array, use `mapfile -t lines < file` (also called `readarray`). Bash arrays are one-dimensional (no arrays inside arrays) and can't be handed on to programs you start.
concepts.code:
cd "$(mktemp -d)"
fruits=(apple "star fruit" kiwi)
fruits+=(mango)
echo "${fruits[1]}"          # star fruit
echo "${#fruits[@]}"         # 4
for f in "${fruits[@]}"; do printf '<%s>' "$f"; done; echo
# <apple><star fruit><kiwi><mango>
echo "${fruits[@]:1:2}"      # star fruit kiwi
unset 'fruits[0]'
echo "${!fruits[@]}"         # 1 2 3  (sparse!)
declare -A port=([http]=80 [https]=443)
port[ssh]=22
echo "${port[https]}"        # 443
[[ -v port[ftp] ]] || echo "no ftp"    # no ftp
for k in "${!port[@]}"; do echo "$k=${port[$k]}"; done   # order not guaranteed
printf 'x\ny\n' > two.txt
mapfile -t lines < two.txt
echo "${#lines[@]} lines, first=${lines[0]}"   # 2 lines, first=x
takeaways: "${arr[@]}" expands each element as one word; always quote it
declare -A for key/value maps; keys come back in no particular order
Build command lines in arrays, then run "${cmd[@]}"
pitfalls: Writing ${arr} or $arr, which gives only the first element.

quiz.q: After `a=(x y z); unset 'a[1]'`, what does ${#a[@]} print?
quiz.explain: Two elements remain (indices 0 and 2); the array is now sparse.

quiz.q: Which expansion keeps 'star fruit' as a single word when passed to a command?
quiz.explain: Quoted [@] expands every element to exactly one word; the others split or join.

concepts.name: case statements and glob patterns
concepts.summary: Match strings against glob patterns with case, and master *, ?, [...] and extended globs.
concepts.why: case is the clean way to choose what to do based on a file's type, a command word or an option.
concepts.body:
**Glob patterns** match text and file names: `*` any run of characters, `?` exactly one character, `[abc]` or `[a-z]` one character from a set, `[!0-9]` one not in the set. When used unquoted as arguments, globs expand to matching file names, sorted; **hidden files** (names starting with `.`) only match if the pattern starts with a dot.

The same patterns drive the **case** statement, which compares one word against a list of patterns and runs the first match:

```bash
case $word in
  pat1|pat2) commands ;;
  *) default ;;
esac
```

`|` separates alternatives, `;;` ends a branch, and `*)` is the catch-all. case is cleaner than a chain of `elif [[ $x == ... ]]` and it's part of the basic shell standard (POSIX), so it also works in plain `sh`.

Useful shell options via `shopt -s`:

- `nullglob`: unmatched globs expand to nothing instead of themselves,
- `globstar`: `**` matches folders at any depth, as in `**/*.py`,
- `dotglob`: include hidden files,
- `extglob`: extended patterns `!(pat)`, `@(a|b)`, `+(pat)`, `*(pat)`, `?(pat)`.

Globs are not regular expressions: `*` alone means "anything", a `.` is just a dot, and you need `[[ =~ ]]` for real regular expressions.
concepts.code:
cd "$(mktemp -d)"
for name in app.tgz main.c 2024.log --help notes.md; do
  case $name in
    *.tar.gz|*.tgz) kind="tarball" ;;
    *.[ch])         kind="C source" ;;
    [0-9]*)         kind="starts with a digit" ;;
    -h|--help)      kind="help flag" ;;
    *)              kind="other" ;;
  esac
  echo "$name: $kind"
done
# app.tgz: tarball / main.c: C source / 2024.log: starts with a digit
# --help: help flag / notes.md: other
shopt -s nullglob extglob globstar
mkdir -p src/lib && touch a.log b.log c.txt src/x.py src/lib/y.py
logs=(*.log); echo "${#logs[@]} logs"   # 2 logs
echo !(*.log|src)                       # c.txt
echo **/*.py                            # src/lib/y.py src/x.py
none=(*.zip); echo "${#none[@]}"        # 0  (thanks to nullglob)
takeaways: * any text, ? one character, [a-z] one character from a set
case word in pat|pat) ... ;; esac picks the first matching pattern
shopt -s nullglob, globstar and extglob unlock safer, richer globs
pitfalls: Treating globs as regexes, e.g. expecting `.*` to mean 'anything'.

quiz.q: Which case pattern matches both 'y' and 'yes' but not 'yellow'?
quiz.explain: | lists alternatives; y* would also match yellow and [yes] matches one character.

quiz.q: What does `shopt -s nullglob` change?
quiz.explain: Without it, a glob with no matches is left as the literal pattern.

concepts.name: Reading input: read and here-docs
concepts.summary: Read text line by line with while read, and feed blocks of text into commands with here-docs and here-strings.
concepts.why: Processing files line by line and writing blocks of text from a script are everyday tasks.
concepts.body:
`read` reads one line from standard input into variables. Always use `read -r` (otherwise backslashes are swallowed). **IFS** is the variable listing the characters used to split a line into words; set it to choose the separator. With `IFS=: read -r a b c` the line is split at colons, and the **last variable gets the rest** of the line.

The standard loop for handling a file line by line is:

```bash
while IFS= read -r line; do ...; done < file
```

`IFS=` keeps spaces at the start and end of each line, `-r` keeps backslashes, and the `< file` after `done` feeds the whole loop. If the last line doesn't end with a line break, add `|| [[ -n $line ]]` to the condition so it's still handled. Use `_` as a throwaway variable for fields you want to skip.

Other useful options: `-p "Name: "` shows a question first, `-s` hides what's typed (for passwords), `-t 5` gives up after 5 seconds, and `-a arr` reads the words into an array.

A **here-document** feeds lines written in the script itself to a command's standard input: `cat <<EOF ... EOF`. Variables and `$( )` expand inside, unless the end word is quoted (`<<'EOF'`), which keeps the text exactly as written: ideal for writing settings files or other scripts. `<<-EOF` removes tabs at the start of lines so you can indent the block. A **here-string** `<<< "$var"` feeds a single piece of text, handy for `read` and `bc`.
concepts.code:
cd "$(mktemp -d)"
printf 'alice 30\nbob 25\n' > people.txt
while read -r name age; do
  echo "$name is $age"
done < people.txt                 # alice is 30 / bob is 25
IFS=: read -r user _ uid _ < /etc/passwd
echo "$user has uid $uid"         # root has uid 0
read -r first rest <<< "one two three"
echo "$first | $rest"             # one | two three
who=World
cat <<EOF
Hello $who, today is $(date +%A)
EOF
cat <<'EOF'
No $expansion here
EOF
# read -rsp "Password: " pw       # interactive: hidden input
takeaways: while IFS= read -r line; do ...; done < file is the line loop
The last variable of read collects the rest of the line
<<EOF expands variables, <<'EOF' is literal, <<< feeds one string
pitfalls: Piping into `while read` and expecting variables set in the loop to survive; the loop runs in a separate copy of the shell (a subshell).

quiz.q: With `IFS=, read -r a b <<< "1,2,3"`, what is b?
quiz.explain: The last variable receives the remainder of the line, including later separators.

quiz.q: How do you stop $HOME from expanding inside a here-document?
quiz.explain: A quoted delimiter makes the whole here-document literal.

concepts.name: Environment variables and startup files
concepts.summary: export, variables for one command, PATH, and which of .bashrc and .bash_profile runs when.
concepts.why: Most 'works in my terminal but not when run automatically' problems come down to the environment.
concepts.body:
Shell variables live only in the current shell. **Exported** variables form the **environment**, which is copied into every program or script you start from this shell (its *child processes*), so they can read them. `export NAME=value` creates and exports in one step; `env` or `printenv` lists the environment. Changes made in a child never flow back to the parent.

Put assignments in front of a command to set them **for that command only**: `TZ=UTC date` or `LC_ALL=C sort file`. This is how you pass settings to a tool without changing your shell.

`PATH` is a list of folders, separated by colons, that bash searches for commands, in order. Add your own with `export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"` (putting it first gives it priority). After installing something new, `hash -r` makes bash forget where it found programs before.

**Startup files** are scripts bash runs by itself when it starts:

- **Login shells** (the first shell after you log in, for example over SSH or at a text console, or `bash -l`) read `/etc/profile`, then the first of `~/.bash_profile`, `~/.bash_login`, `~/.profile`.
- Other shells you type into (most new terminal tabs on Linux) read `~/.bashrc`.
- **Scripts** read neither, unless `BASH_ENV` points at a file.

The usual setup: put aliases, prompt settings and functions in `~/.bashrc`, and make `~/.bash_profile` source it. Programs started automatically, such as scheduled jobs and system services, begin with a minimal environment, so scripts should set the `PATH` and variables they rely on.
concepts.code:
greeting=hi                                 # shell variable only
bash -c 'echo "child sees: [$greeting]"'    # child sees: []
export greeting
bash -c 'echo "child sees: [$greeting]"'    # child sees: [hi]
MODE=fast bash -c 'echo "mode=$MODE"'       # mode=fast  (set for ONE command)
echo "mode=[${MODE:-}]"                     # mode=[]    (not set in this shell)
echo "$PATH" | tr ':' '\n' | head -n 3      # first directories searched
export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"        # prepend your own bin
printenv HOME                               # /home/you
# ~/.bash_profile (login shells) typically contains just:
#   [[ -f ~/.bashrc ]] && . ~/.bashrc
# ~/.bashrc (interactive shells): aliases, prompt, functions
takeaways: export copies a variable into the environment of child processes
VAR=value cmd sets a variable for one command only
Login shells read ~/.bash_profile, interactive ones ~/.bashrc, scripts neither
pitfalls: Putting PATH changes only in ~/.bashrc and wondering why a scheduled job or a code editor doesn't see them.

quiz.q: A script runs `export DEBUG=1`. Is DEBUG set in the terminal that launched the script afterwards?
options: No, environment flows only from parent to child
Only if the script used sudo
Only until the terminal is resized
quiz.explain: The script is a child process; exported variables go to its children, never back to the parent.

quiz.q: Which file does a new interactive, non-login bash on Linux read?
quiz.explain: Interactive non-login shells read ~/.bashrc; login shells read the profile files.

concepts.name: Safer scripts: set -euo pipefail
concepts.summary: Make scripts stop on errors, unset variables and failed pipeline parts, and know where these checks don't apply.
concepts.why: Without these options a script keeps going after a failure and can do real damage with empty variables.
concepts.body:
By default bash ignores failures and keeps running. Three options, usually written together at the top of a script and nicknamed **strict mode**, change that:

- `set -e` (errexit): exit when a command fails.
- `set -u` (nounset): treat expanding an unset variable as an error, which catches typos like `rm -rf "$buidl_dir/"`.
- `set -o pipefail`: a pipeline fails if any part fails, not just the last.

`set -e` deliberately ignores some failures, and you must know which. It does not trigger for commands in an `if`/`while` condition, for any command in a `&&`/`||` list except the last, or for commands negated with `!`. And the status of the command inside `$( )` is lost when it is used in `local x=$(cmd)` or `echo "$(cmd)"`; declare first (`local x`) and assign on its own line.

Commands that legitimately return non-zero need handling: `grep` returns 1 for no match, `diff` for differences. Use `|| true`, or test them in an `if`.

With `-u`, optional arguments and variables need defaults: `"${1:-}"`, `"${DEBUG:-0}"`. Some people also set `IFS=$'\n\t'` so unquoted expansions only split at line breaks and tabs. Strict mode is a safety net, not a substitute for checking the errors you can anticipate and printing helpful messages.
concepts.code:
cd "$(mktemp -d)"
cat > strict.sh <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
name=${1:-world}              # -u: optional args need defaults
echo "hello $name"
count=$(grep -c foo /dev/null || true)   # grep exits 1 on no match
echo "count=$count"
if ! mkdir /proc/x 2>/dev/null; then     # failures inside if are fine
  echo "mkdir failed, handled"
fi
echo "$undefined_var"         # -u: the script dies here
echo "never printed"
EOF
bash strict.sh; echo "exit status: $?"
# hello world / count=0 / mkdir failed, handled
# strict.sh: line 10: undefined_var: unbound variable
# exit status: 1
takeaways: set -euo pipefail: stop on errors, unset variables and failed pipeline parts
-e is suspended in conditions, && / || lists and after !
Give optional variables defaults with ${var:-}
pitfalls: `local out=$(cmd)` hides cmd's failure from set -e because local itself succeeds.

quiz.q: Under `set -e`, does `if grep -q x file; then ...` abort the script when x is not found?
options: No, commands in an if condition are exempt
quiz.explain: errexit ignores failures of commands whose status is being tested.

quiz.q: What does `set -u` catch?
options: Expanding a variable that was never set
quiz.explain: nounset makes expanding an unset variable an error instead of an empty string.

concepts.name: trap: cleanup and signals
concepts.summary: Run cleanup code when a script exits, fails or is interrupted, so scratch files and locks never get left behind.
concepts.why: Real scripts create scratch files, lock files (which stop two copies running at once) and background programs that must be cleaned up even on failure.
concepts.body:
`trap 'commands' SIGNALS` registers code to run when the shell receives a **signal** (a notice from the operating system, such as "stop" when you press Ctrl-C) or reaches a special event. The most useful is **EXIT**, a **pseudo-signal** (a bash-only event) that fires whenever the script ends: normally, through `exit N`, or because `set -e` stopped it. A single EXIT trap is bash's version of `finally` in other languages: code that always runs at the end.

The standard recipe: create scratch files or folders with `mktemp`, then immediately register the trap.

- Put cleanup in a function and register it with `trap cleanup EXIT`.
- Read `$?` as the first thing in the function to know whether the script failed.
- Use `rm -rf -- "$tmpdir"`; the `--` guards against names starting with a dash.

Other events: `INT` (Ctrl-C), `TERM` (a polite "please stop", sent by `kill` or by the system when shutting a service down), `HUP` (terminal closed), and the bash pseudo-signals `ERR` (a command failed) and `DEBUG` (before every command). By convention a script interrupted by a signal exits with 128 + the signal number, so 130 after Ctrl-C.

`trap - INT` restores the default and `trap '' INT` ignores the signal. `trap -p` shows current traps. **SIGKILL** (9) can never be trapped, so no cleanup runs after `kill -9`; design temp files to be harmless if left behind. Subshells don't keep all of the parent's traps, so set them in the process that owns the files.
concepts.code:
cd "$(mktemp -d)"
cat > job.sh <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
tmpdir=$(mktemp -d)
cleanup() {
  local status=$?
  rm -rf -- "$tmpdir"
  echo "cleaned up (exit status $status)" >&2
}
trap cleanup EXIT              # normal exit, error, or exit N
trap 'echo "interrupted" >&2; exit 130' INT TERM
echo "working in $tmpdir"
touch "$tmpdir/data"
false                          # set -e aborts here...
echo "not reached"
EOF
bash job.sh
# working in /tmp/tmp.XXXX
# cleaned up (exit status 1)
takeaways: trap cleanup EXIT runs on every exit path: the shell's finally
Trap INT and TERM to exit cleanly with 128 + the signal's number
SIGKILL cannot be trapped
pitfalls: Registering the trap after creating several resources, so an early failure leaks the first ones.

quiz.q: Which trap runs both on a normal end and when set -e aborts the script?
quiz.explain: EXIT fires on every way the shell exits; ERR only on failures, INT only on Ctrl-C.

quiz.q: A process gets `kill -9`. What happens to its EXIT trap?
options: It runs only if set -e is on
quiz.explain: SIGKILL ends the process immediately; nothing in the process gets to run.

concepts.name: Parsing options with getopts
concepts.summary: Accept -v, -o FILE and bundled flags properly with the getopts builtin and a usage message.
concepts.why: Scripts that accept options the way standard commands do are easier to use and to call from other scripts.
concepts.body:
`getopts optstring var` reads short options (`-v`, `-o file`) one at a time in a `while` loop. The optstring lists the accepted option letters; a letter followed by `:` takes a value, which arrives in `$OPTARG`. A leading `:` switches to silent error mode, where you handle problems yourself: an unknown option sets `var` to `?` and a missing value sets it to `:`, with the offending letter in `$OPTARG`.

getopts handles combined flags (`-vf`), attached values (`-ofile`) and stops at the first non-option or at `--`. After the loop, `shift $((OPTIND - 1))` removes the options already read, so `"$@"` holds only the remaining arguments (file names and the like).

Good habits for a script's options:

- a `usage` function that prints to stderr and exits with status 2,
- defaults set before the loop,
- check the remaining arguments after shifting (`(( $# > 0 )) || usage`),
- support `-h` for help.

getopts is built into bash and every standard (POSIX) shell, so it is portable, but it only understands **short** options. For `--long-options`, either parse manually with a `while (( $# )); do case $1 in ...` loop plus `shift`, or use the util-linux `getopt` program (note: no s), which is available on Linux but differs on macOS.
takeaways: Letters in the optstring are options; a trailing : means it takes a value in $OPTARG
shift $((OPTIND - 1)) leaves only the remaining arguments in "$@"
getopts is short-options only; parse --long options manually
pitfalls: Forgetting the shift after the loop, so the options are processed again as file names.

quiz.q: In the optstring 'ab:c', which option takes an argument?
quiz.explain: The colon after b marks it as requiring a value.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of `shift $((OPTIND - 1))` after a getopts loop?
options: Removes the parsed options so $@ holds the operands
Resets getopts for the next call
quiz.explain: OPTIND points at the first unparsed argument; shifting drops everything before it.

concepts.name: Subshells, grouping and process substitution
concepts.summary: Know when code runs in a subshell, group commands with { } and ( ), and treat command output as a file with <( ).
concepts.why: Lost variable updates and puzzling cd behaviour are almost always subshell effects.
concepts.body:
A **subshell** is a copy of the current shell running as a separate process. It starts with all the variables (exported or not), but nothing it changes, not variables, `cd`, `set` options or other settings, makes it back to the parent. Bash creates subshells for:

- `( commands )` explicit grouping,
- `$( command substitution )`,
- each part of a pipeline (all of them by default),
- commands started in the background with `cmd &`.

`{ commands; }` groups **without** a subshell: same process, so changes stay. Use it to send the output of several commands to one place: `{ date; uname -a; } > info.txt`. Note the required spaces and the final `;`. Use `( )` when you want isolation, such as `(cd build && make)` to change folder temporarily.

The classic mistake is `cmd | while read -r line; do count=$((count+1)); done`: the loop runs in a subshell and `count` is unchanged afterwards. Fix it by feeding the loop from a **process substitution** instead of a pipe: `done < <(cmd)`.

Process substitution `<(cmd)` runs `cmd` and gives you a file name (like `/dev/fd/63`) connected to its output; `>(cmd)` gives a file name that feeds `cmd`'s input. It lets you pass command output to programs that insist on file arguments: `diff <(sort a) <(sort b)`, or `tee >(gzip > log.gz)`.
concepts.code:
(cd /tmp && pwd)                # /tmp   -- subshell: the cd does not leak
pwd                             # unchanged
{ echo one; echo two; } > /tmp/both.txt   # group, same shell, one redirect
count=0
printf 'a\nb\n' | while read -r _; do count=$((count + 1)); done
echo "pipe: $count"             # pipe: 0     (loop ran in a subshell)
count=0
while read -r _; do count=$((count + 1)); done < <(printf 'a\nb\n')
echo "procsub: $count"          # procsub: 2
diff <(printf '1\n2\n3\n') <(printf '1\n3\n')
# 2d1
# < 2
echo <(true)                    # /dev/fd/63  (it is a file name)
x=1; (x=2); echo "x=$x"         # x=1
takeaways: ( ) and pipeline stages run in subshells; their changes are lost
{ ...; } groups in the current shell
<(cmd) turns output into a readable file name; use done < <(cmd)
pitfalls: Incrementing a counter inside `cmd | while read` and reading it after the loop.

quiz.q: Why does `echo hi | read -r v; echo "$v"` print an empty line in bash by default?
options: read ran in a subshell of the pipeline
quiz.explain: Each pipeline stage runs in a subshell, so v is set only there.

quiz.q: Which grouping runs commands in the current shell?
quiz.explain: Braces group without forking; parentheses, $( ) and pipes create subshells.

concepts.name: Background jobs, wait and parallelism
concepts.summary: Run commands in the background with &, wait for them, check how they ended, and run several at once with xargs -P.
concepts.why: Running independent tasks at the same time can turn a ten-minute script into a one-minute one.
concepts.body:
Ending a command with `&` starts it in the **background**: the shell continues immediately and stores the job's process ID in `$!`. `wait` waits until all background jobs finish; `wait "$pid"` waits for one and returns **its exit status**, which is how you detect failures of parallel tasks. Bash 5.1 added `wait -n -p var` to wait for whichever job finishes next and report its PID.

In a terminal you are typing into, **job control** manages jobs: `jobs` lists them, Ctrl-Z suspends the foreground job, `bg` resumes it in the background and `fg %1` brings job 1 back. Background jobs die with the terminal unless started with `nohup` or detached with `disown`; for anything long-running, use a tool built for it, such as tmux or screen (which keep running after you disconnect) or a system service.

For many small tasks, do not start thousands of `&` jobs at once. Limit how many run at once:

- `xargs -P 4 -n 1 cmd` runs up to four commands at a time from input lines (use `-0` with `find -print0` for safe file names),
- GNU `parallel` offers more control,
- or count running jobs and call `wait -n` before starting another.

Output from parallel jobs interleaves unpredictably; write each job's output to its own file, or prefix lines. Remember each background job runs in a subshell, so it cannot set variables in the parent.
concepts.code:
sleep 0.2 & pid1=$!
(sleep 0.1; exit 3) & pid2=$!
wait "$pid2"; echo "job 2 status: $?"   # job 2 status: 3
wait "$pid1"; echo "job 1 status: $?"   # job 1 status: 0
work() { sleep "0.$(( RANDOM % 3 ))"; echo "done $1"; }
for item in a b c; do work "$item" & done
wait                                    # all three done, order varies
printf '%s\n' 1 2 3 4 5 6 |
  xargs -P 3 -I{} sh -c 'sleep 0.1; echo "item {}"'   # 3 at a time
max=2
for n in 1 2 3 4; do
  while (( $(jobs -rp | wc -l) >= max )); do wait -n; done
  work "job$n" &
done
wait
takeaways: cmd & runs in the background; $! is its PID
wait "$pid" returns that job's exit status
Cap concurrency with xargs -P or wait -n
pitfalls: Starting jobs with & and never calling wait, so the script exits before they finish or their failures go unnoticed.

quiz.q: How do you learn whether a background job failed?
quiz.explain: After cmd &, $? is 0 immediately; wait returns the job's real exit status.

quiz.q: What does `xargs -P 4` do?
options: Runs up to 4 commands in parallel
quiz.explain: -P sets the maximum number of processes run at once; -n sets arguments per command.

concepts.name: Debugging and ShellCheck
concepts.summary: Trace scripts with set -x and a better PS4, check syntax with bash -n and catch bugs early with ShellCheck.
concepts.why: Shell mistakes are often silent; printing each command as it runs, and automatic checkers, find them in minutes.
concepts.body:
Bash has built-in tools for seeing what a script really does:

- `bash -n script.sh` parses the script without running anything: a quick syntax check.
- `bash -x script.sh`, or `set -x` inside the script, prints every command after expansion, prefixed with `+`. Turn it off again with `set +x` to trace just one section.
- Customise the prefix with `PS4`: `PS4='+ ${BASH_SOURCE}:${LINENO}:${FUNCNAME[0]:-main}: '` adds file, line and function to each traced line. Use single quotes so it expands at trace time.
- `trap '...' ERR` can report the failing command (`$BASH_COMMAND`) and line (`$LINENO`).
- `set -o functrace` and `set -o errtrace` make DEBUG and ERR traps apply inside functions.

**ShellCheck** is a free checker that reads your script without running it and knows hundreds of shell mistakes: unquoted variables (SC2086), `for f in $(ls)`, useless `cat`, `cd` without error handling, unreachable code, variables used but never assigned, and bash-only features (**bashisms**) in `#!/bin/sh` scripts. Every warning has an ID with a wiki page explaining it. Run it in your editor and in CI (the automatic checks that run on every change); disable a specific check on one line with a `# shellcheck disable=SC2086` comment when you are sure.

For harder problems: print values to stderr with `declare -p var`, and reproduce the issue in a small test script before touching the real one.
concepts.code:
bash -n deploy.sh              # syntax check only, runs nothing
bash -x deploy.sh arg1         # trace every command
# inside a script:
PS4='+ ${BASH_SOURCE}:${LINENO}: '
set -x
total=$(( 2 + 3 ))
# + deploy.sh:6: total=5
set +x
trap 'echo "error at line $LINENO: $BASH_COMMAND" >&2' ERR
declare -p total >&2           # declare -- total="5"
shellcheck deploy.sh
# In deploy.sh line 3:
# rm -rf $dir/*
#        ^--^ SC2086 (info): Double quote to prevent globbing and word splitting.
takeaways: bash -n checks syntax, set -x traces execution
A PS4 with ${LINENO} makes traces readable
Run ShellCheck on every script, in the editor and in CI
pitfalls: Leaving `set -x` on in a script that handles secrets: they are printed in the trace.

quiz.q: What does `bash -n script.sh` do?
options: Runs the script without a shebang
Parses it for syntax errors without executing
Runs it in a new namespace
quiz.explain: -n (noexec) reads and parses commands but does not run them.

quiz.q: Why should PS4 be set with single quotes?
options: Double quotes are not allowed in PS4
So $LINENO expands each time a line is traced, not once at assignment
quiz.explain: With double quotes, LINENO would be expanded once when PS4 is assigned.

concepts.name: The order of expansions and word splitting
concepts.summary: The exact sequence bash applies to every command line, and how IFS, $@ and $* really behave.
concepts.why: Predicting expansion order explains nearly every 'why did bash do that' surprise.
concepts.body:
Bash processes each command line in a fixed order:

- **Brace expansion**: `{a,b}`, `{1..5}`,
- **tilde expansion**: `~`, `~user`,
- **parameter and variable expansion**, **arithmetic expansion**, **command substitution** and **process substitution**, left to right,
- **word splitting** of the unquoted results of those expansions,
- **pathname expansion** (globbing),
- **quote removal**.

Consequences: `{1..$n}` does not work because braces are expanded before variables. Word splitting only applies to the results of expansions, never to literal text, and quoted results are exempt. File names produced by globbing are never split again, so `for f in *` is safe even with spaces.

Splitting uses **IFS** (default space, tab, newline). Whitespace characters in IFS are trimmed and runs of them collapse; other characters such as `,` or `:` delimit exactly, so empty fields are kept. An empty IFS disables splitting entirely; unset IFS behaves like the default.

`"$@"` expands to each positional parameter as a separate word; `"$*"` joins them into one word using the first character of IFS; unquoted `$@` and `$*` are both split and globbed. The same rules apply to `"${arr[@]}"` versus `"${arr[*]}"`. When building a CSV line, `(IFS=,; echo "$*")` is a neat idiom.
concepts.code:
cd "$(mktemp -d)"
n=3
echo {1..$n}            # {1..3}   braces ran before $n was expanded
echo $(seq 1 "$n")      # 1 2 3
IFS=, read -ra parts <<< "a,b,,c"
echo "${#parts[@]}"     # 4  (non-whitespace IFS keeps the empty field)
data="x  y   z"
set -- $data; echo $#   # 3  (whitespace runs collapse)
IFS=: ; set -- $data; echo $#    # 1  (no colon, one word)
unset IFS
touch a.sh b.sh
pat='*.sh'
echo $pat               # a.sh b.sh  (globbing after expansion)
echo "$pat"             # *.sh
show() { printf '[%s]' "$@"; echo; }
set -- "a b" c
show "$@"               # [a b][c]
show "$*"               # [a b c]
show $*                 # [a][b][c]
(IFS=,; echo "$*")      # a b,c
takeaways: Order: brace, tilde, parameter/arithmetic/command, word splitting, globbing, quote removal
Only unquoted expansion results are split and globbed
"$@" keeps arguments separate; "$*" joins them with the first IFS character
pitfalls: Expecting {1..$n} to produce a range; use seq or a C-style for loop.

quiz.q: Why does `echo {1..$n}` print {1..3} rather than 1 2 3?
options: Brace expansion happens before parameter expansion
quiz.explain: When braces are expanded, $n is still literal text, so the sequence is invalid and left alone.

quiz.q: With IFS=, what does splitting `a,,b` produce?
quiz.explain: Non-whitespace IFS characters delimit exactly, so the empty field between the commas is kept.

concepts.name: How bash runs commands: fork and exec
concepts.summary: Command lookup order, builtins versus programs, fork/exec, $$ versus $BASHPID, lastpipe and exec.
concepts.why: Understanding processes explains performance, why cd must be a builtin and where variables go.
concepts.body:
For a simple command name, bash searches in this order: **aliases** (only in a shell you are typing into), **keywords** (`if`, `[[`), **functions**, **builtins**, then bash's memory of where it found programs before (`hash`), and finally the folders in `PATH`. `type -a name` shows every match. `command name` skips functions and aliases; `builtin name` forces the builtin, useful inside a wrapper function of the same name.

An external program runs via a **fork** (the shell makes a copy of its own process) and then an **exec** (the copy swaps itself for the program). The parent waits for it unless it was started with `&`. Builtins run inside the shell process, which is why `cd`, `export`, `read` and `source` must be builtins: they change the shell's own state. It is also why a loop that calls an external program thousands of times is slow and one using parameter expansion is fast.

Subshells are forks without exec. `$$` always holds the main shell's PID, while `$BASHPID` gives the current (sub)shell's PID. Bash forks for each pipeline stage; with `shopt -s lastpipe` (non-interactive shells) the last stage runs in the current shell, so `cmd | read -r v` keeps `v`.

`exec cmd` replaces the shell itself, with no fork and no return. Wrapper scripts, such as the script that starts the main program in a Docker container (its entrypoint), end with `exec "$@"` so the real program becomes process 1 and receives signals directly.
concepts.code:
type -a echo                 # echo is a shell builtin / echo is /usr/bin/echo
echo() { builtin echo "wrapped: $*"; }
echo hi                      # wrapped: hi
command echo hi              # hi   (skips the function)
unset -f echo
echo "main: $$ $BASHPID"     # the same PID twice
( echo "sub:  $$ $BASHPID" ) # $$ unchanged, BASHPID differs
printf 'x\n' | read -r v; echo "v=[$v]"   # v=[]
shopt -s lastpipe            # scripts only: last stage runs here
printf 'x\n' | read -r v; echo "v=[$v]"   # v=[x]
bash -c 'exec echo "replaced"; echo "never printed"'   # replaced
time (for i in {1..200}; do basename /a/b.txt >/dev/null; done)  # slow: 200 forks
time (for i in {1..200}; do : "${p##*/}"; done)                  # fast: no forks
takeaways: Lookup: alias, keyword, function, builtin, hash, PATH
External commands cost a fork and exec; builtins do not
$$ is the main shell, $BASHPID the current subshell; exec replaces the shell
pitfalls: Entrypoint scripts that run the app without exec, leaving the shell as PID 1 that does not forward SIGTERM.

quiz.q: Why must cd be a shell builtin?
options: A child process cannot change its parent's working directory
quiz.explain: An external cd would change only its own process's directory and then exit.

quiz.q: What does a Docker entrypoint script gain by ending with `exec "$@"`?
options: The app replaces the shell and receives signals directly
The script can continue after the app exits
quiz.explain: exec replaces the shell process, so the app becomes PID 1 and gets SIGTERM itself.

concepts.name: File descriptors and exec redirections
concepts.summary: Open, duplicate, swap and close file descriptors, send a whole script's output somewhere, and use coprocesses.
concepts.why: Advanced logging, locking and two-way communication all rely on managing descriptors yourself.
concepts.body:
Redirections on `exec` without a command apply to the **current shell** for the rest of the script:

- `exec 3> file` opens fd 3 for writing, `exec 3< file` for reading, `exec 3<> file` both,
- `exec 3>&-` closes it,
- `exec {fd}> file` lets bash choose a free number (10 or above) and stores it in `fd`; use `>&"$fd"`.

Duplication `n>&m` makes fd n a copy of fd m **at that moment**, which explains classic tricks. `cmd 2>&1 >/dev/null` sends only stderr into a pipe and discards stdout. `3>&1 1>&2 2>&3 3>&-` swaps stdout and stderr through a spare descriptor.

`exec > >(tee -a run.log) 2>&1` near the top of a script copies all following output to a log file while still showing it. Because `tee` runs alongside the script rather than inside it, its last lines can appear after the script exits.

Descriptors also power locking: `exec 9> /var/lock/job.lock; flock -n 9 || exit 1` ensures only one instance runs, and the lock is released automatically when the process exits.

`coproc NAME { cmd; }` starts a background process with two pipes; write to `${NAME[1]}` and read from `${NAME[0]}`. Watch for buffering: many programs only flush output when their input closes. Inspect a process's descriptors in `/proc/$$/fd`.
concepts.code:
cd "$(mktemp -d)"
exec 3> log.txt                # fd 3 stays open for the rest of the script
echo "to the log" >&3
exec 3>&-                      # close it
cat log.txt                    # to the log
exec {fd}< /etc/passwd         # bash picks a free fd number
read -r first <&"$fd"; exec {fd}<&-
echo "${first%%:*}"            # root
{ echo out; echo err >&2; } 2>&1 >/dev/null | tr a-z A-Z   # ERR
{ echo out; echo err >&2; } 3>&1 1>&2 2>&3 3>&- | cat   # err via the pipe, out on stderr
exec 9> job.lock
flock -n 9 && echo "got the lock"   # got the lock
coproc UP { tr a-z A-Z; }
echo "hello coproc" >&"${UP[1]}"; exec {UP[1]}>&-
read -r line <&"${UP[0]}"; echo "$line"   # HELLO COPROC
ls /proc/$$/fd                 # 0 1 2 9 255 ...  (open descriptors)
takeaways: exec with only redirections changes the current shell's descriptors
n>&m copies m at that moment; order explains 2>&1 >/dev/null
flock on an fd gives easy single-instance locking
pitfalls: Expecting `cmd >/dev/null 2>&1` and `cmd 2>&1 >/dev/null` to be the same.

quiz.q: What reaches the pipe in `cmd 2>&1 >/dev/null | less`?
quiz.explain: First stderr is pointed at the pipe (current stdout), then stdout is moved to /dev/null.

quiz.q: What does `exec 3>&-` do?
quiz.explain: >&- closes the given descriptor.

concepts.name: POSIX sh, bashisms and when to stop
concepts.summary: Know which features are bash-only, how /bin/sh differs across systems and when a script should become Python.
concepts.why: Scripts run in Alpine containers, on macOS and under dash; knowing the boundaries prevents 'works on my machine'.
concepts.body:
`/bin/sh` is not bash everywhere: it is **dash** on Debian and Ubuntu, BusyBox **ash** in Alpine images and bash in POSIX mode on RHEL. macOS ships an old **bash 3.2** (zsh is its default shell), which lacks associative arrays, `mapfile`, `${var,,}` and `wait -n`. A script with `#!/bin/sh` must stick to POSIX shell.

Common **bashisms** and their POSIX replacements:

- `[[ ]]` becomes `[ ]` with careful quoting, or `case` for patterns,
- arrays become the single list `"$@"` (via `set --`) or newline-separated strings,
- `(( ))` becomes `$(( ))` inside `[ ]`; `function f` becomes `f()`,
- `&>` becomes `> f 2>&1`; `source` becomes `.`; `$'\t'` becomes `printf`,
- `<( )` has no equivalent; use scratch files or named pipes (FIFOs).

Check portability with `shellcheck --shell=sh`, `checkbashisms`, or simply run the script with `dash`. If you need bash, say so with `#!/usr/bin/env bash` and, if necessary, guard on `BASH_VERSINFO`.

Know when to stop. Shell is excellent for gluing commands together, but once a script passes a couple of hundred lines, manipulates structured data (JSON, CSV with quoting), needs real error handling, floats or unit tests, a language like Python or Go will be shorter and safer. Keep the shell part a thin wrapper.
concepts.code:
# Bash only                          # POSIX sh equivalent
# [[ $x == a* ]] && echo yes        # case $x in a*) echo yes ;; esac
# (( n++ ))                          # n=$((n + 1))
# lower=${s,,}                       # lower=$(printf '%s' "$s" | tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]')
# cmd &> out.log                     # cmd > out.log 2>&1
# source ./lib.sh                    # . ./lib.sh
# arr=(a b c); "${arr[@]}"           # set -- a b c; "$@"
if (( BASH_VERSINFO[0] < 4 )); then  # macOS /bin/bash is 3.2
  echo "this script needs bash >= 4" >&2
  exit 1
fi
printf 'x=1; [[ $x == 1 ]] && echo ok\n' > /tmp/t.sh
bash /tmp/t.sh                       # ok
dash /tmp/t.sh 2>&1 || true          # /tmp/t.sh: 1: [[: not found
takeaways: /bin/sh may be dash, ash or bash in POSIX mode; macOS bash is 3.2
Test portability with shellcheck --shell=sh or by running dash
Move to Python or Go when logic, data or size outgrow the shell
pitfalls: Writing bash features in a script whose shebang is #!/bin/sh: it works on RHEL and fails on Ubuntu.

quiz.q: A #!/bin/sh script using [[ ]] works on Fedora but fails on Ubuntu. Why?
options: Ubuntu's /bin/sh is dash, which has no [[
quiz.explain: On Debian-based systems sh is dash, a strict POSIX shell; on Fedora sh is bash.

quiz.q: Which feature is NOT available in macOS's default /bin/bash 3.2?
quiz.explain: Associative arrays arrived in bash 4.0.
